content: People who inject drugs (PWID) are a key population at particularly high risk of acquiring hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infections. In many high-income countries and some developing nations, the ongoing transmission of HCV is primarily driven by the PWID population. A global review of data from 77 countries estimated that HCV exposure (anti-HCV positive) among PWID ranges between 60% and 80% in 25 countries and exceeds 80% in 12 countries. Similarly, the prevalence of HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) among PWID varies significantly. In 21 countries, the prevalence ranges from 5% to 10%, while in 10 countries, it exceeds 10%. Men who have sex with men (MSM) are also at risk of acquiring HBV and HCV through sexual transmission. MSM populations often exhibit higher rates of HBV infection, necessitating targeted HBV screening and vaccination efforts. HIV-positive MSM are at a significantly higher risk of acquiring HCV compared to their HIV-negative counterparts. Sex workers represent another key population at high risk of HBV and HCV infections. Factors contributing to their vulnerability include unsafe working conditions, barriers to consistent condom use, and limited access to healthcare services. Migrants and refugees are also disproportionately affected by viral hepatitis due to various factors, including limited access to healthcare and higher rates of injecting drug use in some settings. Prison populations are particularly vulnerable to HBV, HCV, and HIV infections. Globally, the prevalence of these infections in prisons is estimated to be two to ten times higher than in the general population, and in some settings, it can be up to 50 times higher. This elevated risk is often attributed to the sharing of needles, syringes, and other injecting equipment, compounded by the lack of access to clean needles and prevention tools in prison settings. Indigenous populations in certain regions are disproportionately affected by viral hepatitis and other health issues. Contributing factors include higher rates of injecting drug use and increased incarceration rates among indigenous individuals. The epidemiological patterns of HBV and HCV infections vary by region. For example, in Africa, most HBV infections are acquired perinatally or during childhood, resulting in a generalized high prevalence across the population. In contrast, in the South-East Asia region, PWID and MSM exhibit higher prevalence rates compared to the general population. Community-based testing approaches, such as outreach and mobile testing, have demonstrated benefits, including earlier diagnosis and access to treatment before the development of complications like cirrhosis. These approaches are particularly effective in reaching key populations and individuals who are asymptomatic or unlikely to seek care at healthcare facilities. However, challenges include suboptimal linkage to care and variable positivity rates in certain settings. Provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in healthcare facilities is another effective strategy, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Key populations, such as PWID, MSM, and sex workers, are disproportionately affected by hepatitis and are less likely to have received HBV vaccination. Offering HBV testing and vaccination to these groups can facilitate higher vaccination completion rates. Partner testing for HBV and HCV has several benefits, including the adoption of prevention strategies by couples, improved linkage to care, and increased awareness of HBV and HCV status, particularly among men. Offering partner testing also provides an opportunity for counseling on risk reduction and vaccination. Cost-effectiveness studies on HBV screening and treatment are limited, particularly in LMICs. Most available data come from high-income countries with low HBV prevalence. The cost of antiviral drugs, adherence to treatment, and linkage to care are key determinants of the cost-effectiveness of screening and treatment strategies. Community-based screening programs, such as the PROLIFICA study in The Gambia, have demonstrated the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of large-scale screening and treatment interventions in LMIC settings. In conclusion, while the evidence base for the cost-effectiveness of HBV screening remains limited, particularly in LMICs, targeted testing and treatment strategies are likely to be worthwhile. These strategies should prioritize key populations and ensure equitable access to care in supportive, stigma-free environments.
